title: Almost perfect!
text:
I enjoy using this app a lot and would give it 5 starts if it wasn’t for 2 missing features I use daily in other apps.

1. The ability to separate focus point and exposure. For example, in Moment, you can double tap the screen to separate the focus and the exposure. It very useful when you want to focus on something but not blow out the background. Then you can use the EV slider if needed. 

2. The ability to dial down the intensity of a Look. Many times a Look can be too strong for a specific scene. The ability to lower their intensity for example Dawn 70% or Nova 35%. This feature alone would make a huge difference. 

If Halide had this 2 features, Halide would be my everyday camera. No need for Lightroom or any other app. 

If at least on of these features gets added, it would get 5 stars!

title: Masters of Marketing Comms & Cons
text:
This dev shop is adept at coming up with clever marketing terms for features that are mere gimmicks. A few years ago, they debuted ‘Instant Raw’, which never worked. More recently they’ve released ‘Process Zero’, which is essentially their opinionated version of RAW with limitations. IMO, it results in worse images with no benefits. Finally, they have ‘Image Lab’, which is merely an exposure adjustment. One of the founders of Halide has a personal website in which he charges up to $1500 per month for access to a photography course, premium articles, and limited merch drops. Thus far, he hasn’t delivered on any of the aforementioned promises.

In their Discord, they recently stated if you ask any questions about the upcoming version, that we’ve already covered, you’ll be banned from our Discord. Talk about not appreciating your users.

And $10 per month for an iPhone photo app is asinine.

title: Founder bans paying customers for feature requests
text:
I visited Halide’s subreddit once to raise an issue about lack of ability to capture long exposures (5+ second shutter speed). For this, I was banned by Halide’s cofounder, and all my relevant comments were deleted. 

I saw it often mentioned that older phones don’t support this or that due to hardware limitations, so I freshly bought an iPhone 17 Pro to get the full advantage of the latest camera capabilities. Disappointingly, it turned out that Halide lacks feature parity even with the built-in Camera app, which has raw long exposures through Night mode. For a professional photography app, it’s a pretty essential feature. 

The development’s team response basically was to:

1) Tell me to buy Spectre, another app of theirs which has long exposures as a paid-only feature.

2) Blame Apple, saying they do not expose an API to do this. They claimed that Night mode computationally merges exposures, as there is a hard limit of 1 second, and it is somehow not available to Halide.

3) Blame sensor noise issues.

Halide’s founder Ben Sandofsky has personally deleted all of my comments AND permabanned me from the subreddit after I politely (albeit with increased frustration, as they could have simply said “it’s not on the roadmap” instead of grasping at excuses and being condescending to a professional paying customer) addressed each of their points, e.g.:

— I bought Spectre back when it was initially released, and I stated that I own both apps. Spectre is marketed by Halide as an “AI photography app” and does not have raw output (both no-go for professional purposes).

— Apple does expose an API to obtain raw pixel data. Even if there is a hard limit of 1 sec, additively merging raw pixel values (deterministically, no “AI” black magic required) from N shorter back-to-back exposures without leaving raw scene-referred domain is a solved problem (see e.g. Siril, a desktop astrophotography app).

— Noise is not a concern when it comes to raw photography (like the Bayer pattern, the point is to let this be handled by post-processing toolchain).

It is pretty telling that they would upsell their other product, blame Apple, and ban a paying customer once they run out of actual technical arguments.

That said, Halide isn’t really a daily-use app for me. You do need to play around a bit to get comfortable, but overall it’s fairly user-friendly. My main frustration has been performance: after just a handful of photos the app lags, my device heats up, and the app sometimes crashes. Many sessions ended with “issues saving to photo library.” The “rescued photos” option is a lifesaver, but the reliability gap is still disappointing—especially on an iPhone 14 Pro Max.

For the price, I don’t find it worth subscribing as an average user. I see the value for more professional photographers, or people wanting to move in that direction, especially in indoor or more controlled settings. title: A five star app hobbled by one critical missing feature
text:
I can’t say enough good things about Halide. By every measure it should be an amazing five star app. Alas, it’s missing one utterly basic feature that so many other iPhone camera apps have: exposure bracketing. 

The Halide interface is excellent and well thought out. It’s possible to create very high resolution images by shooting raw files in Halide and then stitching them together later on with software like PTGui Pro. But I recently had an experience where I lost a critical image simply because there’s no exposure bracketing. The sunlight was so bright I couldn’t see my screen well, and I therefore didn’t notice that Halide was overexposing the entire scene. I lost an image that could have been very good because all the critical highlights got totally blown out, even shooting raw. Simple exposure bracketing - which I use as a matter of course on my medium format camera (which, alas, I didn’t have with me) - would have saved the day. 

Add exposure bracketing, and Halide becomes not just a five star app but a ten star app. Without that features, it’s hobbled in a way it shouldn’t be.

title: Not a pro. Just some observation.
text:
Pros: 
-provide manual control to iphone specially the older model which gave some focus control. (However it will not change the minimum focus distance of the camera so dont expect some great macro shots if your camera does not natively support it)
-creates raw files even to an older iphone 13mini

Cons:
-the app drains the battery quick 
-app uses a lot of cpu resources
-picture file size are huge even if you set it to heic/apple processed compared to the stock camera(however if you did, it defeats the purpose of no ai filter. You can only do it if you set it in raw which will create a more larger file)
-not ideal if you want to do point and shoot
-hit and miss regarding the no ai filter result
-the live image in the screen is not accurate when you click and take the shots.(especially of you set the shutter speed to slow, fps drops too, which emulate the real camera but painful to use as the phone struggles in the dark. The picture is bright but once taken the the picture is not as accurate as it has been on the live screen before taking the shot)

Conclusion:
The halide is an expensive glorified camera app with a modern skin but still a stock camera underneath.  It will give you some extra manual controls and raw files but will not make up for the hardware limitation especially from the older device. You will have an extra fancy option of histogram, peaking and rule of third with haptic feedback. You can compose the picture that you want but bear in mind that it will take a bit of time, battery and lot of patience to experiment various setting and scenarios. So if you do not have these 3, then you are good with the good ole stock camera. After all it is reliable and free, just a bit processed and less control.

Developing a camera app probably isn’t easy and going up against a free alternative that’s pre-installed on everyone’s phone is tough, that’s the reason $60 seems so expensive for this app; your competition’s price tag is bundled into the hardware. Think about all that’s needed to read camera sensors and adjust exposure due to things like light levels, motion, focal length and more. The problem is that there just isn’t a ton of value in switching over to a new camera app considering it only has about 3 more features, two of which you’ll probably only use once (manual focus & manual exposure) and one that’s only a marginal improvement over the stock app (RAW vs HEIC)(I was not super impressed with the raw photos from this app). The value proposition just doesn’t really make sense here for what you’re getting, and the only reason you would consider getting the app is because Apple paywalls ProRAW behind their high end pricey phones for no reason (other than money). I hate to say it because there was clearly a lot of work put into this app, but it should not exist, and that’s the reason why they don’t make an official hallide camera app for Android. Apple’s anti-consumer practices are the only reason this app exists.

title: Halide: L'App Amata dagli Esteti, un Incubo per chi Scatta Davvero.
text:
Sulla carta, e spinta da un marketing impeccabile, Halide Mark II ha tutto ciò che un fotografo che usa l'iPhone potrebbe desiderare: scatto in ProRAW, controlli manuali completi, focus peaking. L'ho scaricata con aspettative altissime, pronto a trasformare il mio telefono nello strumento professionale definitivo. La promessa, però, si è infranta al primo tocco, lasciando spazio a una frustrazione che non provavo da tempo.
Il problema di Halide non è la sua potenza, ma la sua filosofia. Una filosofia minimalista che, per chiunque abbia passato anni con una vera fotocamera in mano, risulta semplicemente insopportabile. Il mio background è quello delle reflex e delle mirrorless, un mondo dove scattare in manuale significa avere il pieno controllo tattile e, soprattutto, visivo. Il mio cervello è "cablato" per cercare un "cruscotto" di informazioni: l'istogramma in un angolo, i valori ISO e dei tempi ben visibili, un'icona chiara per ogni funzione. Questo non è disordine, è controllo.
Halide fa l'esatto opposto: nasconde tutto. Affida funzioni essenziali a "gesture" da indovinare, costringendoti a fare swipe e tap alla cieca per cambiare un'impostazione che su una reflex avresti regolato in un decimo di secondo con una ghiera. Per un utente come me, questo non è "pulizia", è un handicap. È come chiedere a un pilota di guidare senza cruscotto. E la scelta di bloccare il formato di scatto in 4:3, imponendo un ritaglio in post-produzione, è l'apice dell'arroganza progettuale, una decisione che va contro la prima regola della fotografia: la composizione in-camera.
Ed è qui che il marketing, a mio avviso, vince sulla realtà. Halide viene venduta come l'app "professionale" per eccellenza, ma sembra dimenticare cosa significhi per un professionista avere il controllo. Sembra progettata più per un esteta del design che per un fotografo sul campo. Un professionista non ha tempo per indovinare i gesti, ha bisogno di efficienza, chiarezza e feedback immediato. Tutte cose che questa interfaccia sacrifica sull'altare del minimalismo.

Conclusione: La tecnologia di scatto di Halide sarà anche da 5 stelle, ma se l'esperienza d'uso che ti porta a quella tecnologia è da 1 stella, lo strumento è un fallimento. Per me, lo è stato. Lo strumento si deve adattare al fotografo, non il contrario. Se venite dal mondo delle reflex e amate il controllo, state alla larga: questa app vi farà solo innervosire.

title: Necessita miglioramenti

title: NON CI SIAMO
text:
Fino ad ora niente ha giustificato il prezzo medio-alto di Halide.
Non è l'unica a disporre di controlli manuali, altre app offrono all'utente ancora più libertà d'azione.
Nonostante sia stato fatto un aggiornamento, le foto scattate in modalità RAW appaiono ancora sgranate e di qualità più bassa rispetto alle foto normali (jpg), non solo nel rullino della stessa app e in quello di iPhone, ma anche processandole in altre app di editing: in realtà durante il processo di editing la quantità di elementi (luci e colori) su cui lavorare sembrerebbe quella di un RAW, quindi molte più informazioni rispetto ad un fole jpg, ma l'effetto low-quality persiste anche in fase di esportazione, dando così un resa visiva dell'immagine finale (come anche di quella iniziale del resto) pessima.

title: It can be improved
text:
The application is not bad, it has many options and at the same time it tries to keep a minimalistic design.
I would suggest adding the possibility to control the shutter speed. 
Moreover it would be better if - once finished with the regulations-  the camera went simply full screen without any icon.
